title: Why It Is Called Least Squares
scopeNote: This keeps the original's hand-fitting interaction and adds the residual squares themselves, which is the one place in this batch where the simplified version does more than its parent rather than less. The prediction exercise, the numeric target challenge and the standard error of the estimate stay in the longer version, and the page says so.
summary: Twelve observations and a line set by hand with two sliders. Every residual gets a real square whose area is the residual squared, so the quantity being minimised is drawn rather than described, and the exact least-squares solution is revealed only after the learner has tried.
learningObjectives: State what the intercept and the slope each do to a fitted line.
Explain what least squares minimises, and why the squares are literal.
Explain that exactly one line minimises the total, and that it is computed rather than searched for.
Interpret R squared as a comparison against predicting the mean, including when it is negative.
Explain what a good fit does not establish.
interactionTypes: two range inputs setting a line by hand
a real square drawn on every residual, updating live
a running total of the drawn area against the smallest possible
a withheld reveal of the exact least-squares solution
R squared allowed to go negative rather than floored at zero
privacy: Nothing is collected, stored or transmitted. Everything is computed in the browser and is gone when the page is closed.
accessibilityNotes: Keyboard operable throughout, with both coefficients as labelled range inputs reporting their value in text. The figure description gives the current intercept and slope, the total area, the smallest possible total, R squared and, crucially, the exact best-fitting coefficients, so a learner using a screen reader can reach the answer the same way a sighted learner can. The running total is also printed beside the plot and repeated in the tiles and in a full written sentence beneath them, so nothing depends on judging areas by eye. The figure scrolls sideways rather than shrinking below legible label sizes on a narrow screen. Changes are announced through a polite live region. No timed content and no motion.
dataStatus: Simulated and illustrative. Twelve fictional observations generated from a constant seed, so every learner sees the same data and a lecturer can quote the same answer: an intercept of 20.6 and a slope of 0.49, leaving a total of 1209. Variable X and Variable Y are deliberately unnamed.
simulationNotes: The plot area is square and both axes run 0 to 100 across the same number of viewBox units. That is not a stylistic choice: a square of side e in data units is only drawn as a square on screen when one unit of X and one unit of Y are the same number of pixels, and if that ever changes the squares become rectangles and the activity loses its point. The least-squares coefficients are computed in closed form rather than searched for, which is itself part of the lesson. The slider steps are too coarse to reach that exact pair, so the reveal aims at the best pair the controls can actually produce, found by evaluating all 2501 settings the two sliders admit. Rounding each coefficient independently does not give that pair, because the two are correlated. R squared is deliberately not floored at zero: seeing it go negative is what makes clear that it is a comparison against predicting the mean rather than a percentage of something absolute.
readmeTopic: what least squares actually minimises, drawn as the squares it is named after
